goal: Standardize pricing-service on one test framework for its Python test suite so that tests, CI, and onboarding documentation stay coherent going forward.
question: Select the test framework that pricing-service should use going forward, given that the project is a small Python package (Python >=3.10, no runtime dependencies) whose existing suite, dev dependency pin, GitHub Actions workflow, and onboarding docs are already written for pytest.
known_constraints: The only dev dependency today is pytest>=8; there are no runtime dependencies (pyproject.toml).
CI runs on push on ubuntu-latest, installs -e .[dev], and invokes the suite with a single headless `pytest` command (.github/workflows/ci.yml).
The README states all tests run under pytest in CI and that the suite and onboarding docs assume pytest (README.md:3-4).
The current suite is one test module using @pytest.mark.parametrize (tests/test_pricing.py).
Changing the framework going forward may update tests, pyproject dev extras, the CI workflow, and the README; the current pytest-based state itself is not a mandate.

environment.ci: GitHub Actions, ubuntu-latest, trigger on push
environment.suite_size: one test module, two parametrized cases

evidence: pyproject.toml requires Python >=3.10 and lists pytest>=8 as the sole dev dependency (pyproject.toml:4,8).
The test module imports pytest and uses @pytest.mark.parametrize (tests/test_pricing.py:1,6).
CI installs -e .[dev] and runs `pytest` as a single headless command on ubuntu-latest (.github/workflows/ci.yml:8-9).
The README says all tests run under pytest in CI and that the suite and onboarding docs assume pytest (README.md:3-4).
PyPI metadata (checked 2026-10-01 via https://pypi.org/pypi/pytest/json): pytest 8.0.0 and 8.3.0 declare requires_python >=3.8, 8.4.2 declares >=3.9, and the latest release 9.1.1 declares >=3.10.
Local runtime check: the interpreter is Python 3.14.7 (>=3.10) and the stdlib unittest module is importable.
Local runtime check: `python3 -m unittest --help` exits 0, confirming a non-interactive stdlib CLI runner.

alternatives.name: Keep pytest
alternatives.description: Retain pytest>=8 as the project's test framework, leaving the existing test module, dev dependency pin, CI invocation, and README guidance as they are.
advantages: Existing test module, dev dependency pin, CI workflow, and README guidance need no changes.
Parametrize, fixtures, markers, and a large plugin ecosystem remain available as the suite grows.
The README-documented workflow (pytest in CI; docs assume pytest) stays accurate.
pytest releases from 8.0 onward support Python >=3.10 per PyPI metadata.
disadvantages: Keeps a third-party test dependency in the dev extra that must track upstream releases and breaking changes.
Test code is coupled to a pytest-specific API (@pytest.mark.parametrize).
assumptions: Upstream pytest continues to publish releases supporting the project's Python floor.
The suite will eventually benefit from fixtures or plugins as it grows.

alternatives.name: Migrate to stdlib unittest
alternatives.description: Rewrite the suite as unittest.TestCase tests, remove pytest from the dev extra, and run CI with `python -m unittest`.
advantages: Removes the only third-party dev dependency; tests run on any CPython >=3.10 interpreter.
Unaffected by third-party framework release cadence or breaking changes.
`python -m unittest` provides a single non-interactive CLI command suitable for CI gating.
Stdlib API is stable across Python releases.
disadvantages: Requires rewriting the existing test module from @pytest.mark.parametrize to subTest or loops.
Forfeits pytest fixtures, the plugin ecosystem, and pytest's assertion introspection; failure output is less detailed.
CI workflow, pyproject dev extra, README, and onboarding docs must all be updated together.
TestCase style is more verbose for parameterized cases.
assumptions: The suite does not need pytest-specific plugins or fixtures in the foreseeable future.
`python -m unittest` satisfies the CI gating requirement.

alternatives.name: unittest tests with pytest runner
alternatives.description: Author tests with stdlib unittest.TestCase APIs while keeping pytest>=8 in the dev extra as the CI runner for execution and reporting.
advantages: Test code avoids pytest-specific APIs, so tests remain runnable under `python -m unittest` without pytest installed.
CI keeps pytest's execution, reporting, and plugin ecosystem.
Both the stdlib runner and pytest stay available to contributors.
disadvantages: Maintains the third-party pytest dependency that a stdlib-only setup would remove.
Requires rewriting the existing test module to unittest idioms while tooling and docs still center on pytest.
Forfeits pytest-specific authoring features (fixtures, parametrize) in test code while still carrying pytest as a dependency.
assumptions: Contributors benefit from being able to run tests without installing pytest.
pytest's value as a runner alone justifies keeping the dev dependency.

criteria.name: Suite, CI, and docs continuity
rubric: Requires rewriting the entire suite plus CI and doc changes
Requires rewriting most tests plus CI and doc changes
Requires moderate migration across suite, CI, and docs
Requires only minor edits to suite, CI, or docs
Suite, CI, and onboarding docs work unchanged

criteria.name: Testing capability for a growing suite
rubric: No fixtures, no parameterization, no plugin ecosystem
Parameterization or fixtures, but not both
Fixtures and parameterization with a small plugin ecosystem
Fixtures, parameterization, large plugin ecosystem, and detailed failure reporting

criteria.name: Dependency and maintenance overhead
rubric: Adds several new third-party test dependencies
Adds one new third-party test dependency
Keeps the current single third-party dev dependency
Removes the third-party dev dependency entirely (stdlib only)

criteria.name: Onboarding and documentation alignment
rubric: Docs must be rewritten and contributors must learn an unfamiliar framework
Docs need substantial updates and contributors lose an established workflow
Docs need targeted updates and the workflow stays broadly familiar
Docs stay accurate with small updates
Docs stay accurate unchanged and contributors keep the established workflow

hard_constraints.description: The chosen framework must run on Python >=3.10, the support floor declared in pyproject.toml.
The chosen framework must run the full suite non-interactively from a single CLI command in the existing GitHub Actions CI on ubuntu-latest.

evidence_records.fact: pricing-service declares requires-python = ">=3.10", has no runtime dependencies, and pins pytest>=8 as its only dev dependency.
PyPI metadata: pytest 8.0.0 and 8.3.0 declare requires_python >=3.8, 8.4.2 declares >=3.9, and the latest release 9.1.1 declares >=3.10, so every release from 8.0 onward supports Python 3.10.
The unittest module ships in the CPython standard library and imports successfully on the local Python 3.14.7 interpreter, which satisfies the project's >=3.10 floor.
evidence_records.source: local runtime check: python3 --version and import unittest (Python 3.14.7)

evidence_records.fact: The standard library provides a non-interactive CLI test runner: `python -m unittest --help` exits 0 on the local interpreter.
evidence_records.source: local runtime check: python3 -m unittest --help (exit code 0)

evidence_records.fact: The GitHub Actions workflow installs `-e .[dev]` and runs the suite with a single headless `pytest` command on ubuntu-latest, triggered on push.
The README states that all tests run under pytest in CI and that the suite and onboarding docs assume pytest.
The only test module imports pytest and parameterizes its two cases with @pytest.mark.parametrize.
